definition: A computer that keeps its program as numbers in memory and fetches instructions from there, so changing the program means changing memory contents rather than rewiring hardware.
example: The Manchester Baby of 1948 was an early electronic stored-program computer.

definition: A computer design in which instructions and data share one memory and one path to the CPU. It makes code-as-data easy (loaders, JIT compilers) but means instruction fetches and data accesses compete for the same memory bus.
example: A program can write bytes into memory and later jump to them, because code and data live in the same store.

definition: An experimental computer built at the University of Manchester that ran its first program on 21 June 1948, an early demonstration of an electronic stored-program machine with read/write memory.

The CPU register or architectural state identifying an instruction address. Branches, calls and returns change the instruction stream; the exact current/next-instruction reference point depends on the architecture.
example: An A64 ADR refers to its own instruction address; an x86-64 RIP-relative memory operand uses the following instruction address.

definition: x86’s name for the program counter; the 64-bit version is the register RIP. Code can refer to data at a fixed distance from it (RIP-relative addressing).
An x86-64 addressing form that adds a signed 32-bit displacement to the address of the next instruction. It lets code find nearby data wherever the program is loaded.
example: `[rip + table]` reaches anything within about ±2 GiB of the instruction.

definition: In the textbook CPU model, the register that holds the instruction currently being decoded and executed. Real pipelined cores track many instructions in flight instead of one.
A small, very fast storage slot inside the CPU that instructions read and write directly. Baseline x86-64 has 16 general-purpose 64-bit integer registers and ARM64 has 31.
example: `add rax, rdi` adds the values in two registers without touching memory.

definition: The set of CPU registers an ISA provides, or the hardware array that holds them. A larger register file lets compilers keep more values out of memory.
The arithmetic logic unit: the part of the CPU that adds, subtracts, compares and does bitwise operations on numbers.
The part of the CPU that decodes each instruction and sends the signals that make registers, the ALU and memory do the right thing in the right order.
The basic loop a CPU repeats: fetch the instruction at the program counter, advance the program counter, work out what the instruction means, then carry it out.
A signal, for example from a timer or a device, that makes the CPU pause the current program, save enough state to resume, and run a handler (usually in the kernel).
example: A timer interrupt every few milliseconds lets the operating system take the CPU back from a program stuck in a loop.

definition: Rules that let the CPU or operating system temporarily ignore (mask) some interrupts, or rank them by priority, so an interrupt is only taken when it is eligible.
Scheduling in which the operating system can take the CPU away from a running program, typically on a timer interrupt, without the program having to give it up voluntarily.
A register that collects the result of arithmetic: each operation combines a value with the accumulator and leaves the answer there. Early and very simple machines often had just one.
example: In the lesson’s toy machine, ADD 21 adds the value in cell 21 to the accumulator.

definition: The part of a machine instruction that says which operation to perform, as opposed to the operands it works on.
example: In the toy machine, 221 has opcode 2 (ADD) and address 21.

definition: A value or location an instruction works on: a register, a constant (immediate) or a memory address.
example: In `add rax, rdi` the operands are rax and rdi.

definition: In this module’s toy machine, opcode 0 stops the interpreter. Real x86 HLT instead puts a logical processor into a halted state until an eligible wake event; it is privileged and does not terminate an ordinary user program.
In the lesson’s toy machine, opcode 1: copy the value at a memory address into the accumulator.
In the lesson’s toy machine, opcode 4: copy the accumulator into a memory cell.
An instruction that adds two values. In the toy machine, ADD adds a memory cell to the accumulator; on x86-64 and ARM64 `add` adds registers, immediates or (x86 only) a memory operand.
An instruction that subtracts one value from another. In the toy machine SUB subtracts a memory cell from the accumulator; on x86 `sub rax, rdi` computes rax minus rdi into rax.

Jump if zero: x86 JZ/JE tests the zero flag left by a flag-setting instruction. In this module’s toy machine JZ instead directly tests whether the accumulator is zero; intervening flag-changing operations matter on real x86.
An unconditional jump: it always writes a new address into the program counter, so execution continues there.

Code that changes instruction bytes while the program runs. Permissions, instruction visibility and coordination with executing threads determine whether an update is allowed and safe; the required maintenance depends on the platform.
How a particular processor implements an instruction set inside: its pipeline, caches, predictors and execution units. Two chips with the same ISA can have very different microarchitectures.
example: AMD Zen and Intel Core are different microarchitectures for x86-64.

definition: The ability to run an already-compiled program unchanged. It needs the same ISA features plus a compatible OS, ABI, executable format and libraries.
example: An ARM64 macOS binary is not binary compatible with ARM64 Linux, despite the shared ISA.

definition: A byte order in which the least significant byte of a multi-byte number is stored at the lowest address (big-endian puts the most significant byte first). x86-64 is little-endian.
example: The 32-bit value 0x12345678 is stored as the bytes 78 56 34 12 on a little-endian machine.

definition: Placing a value at an address that is a multiple of some number, usually its size or a power of two. ABIs and some instructions require it; misaligned data can be slower or fault.
example: An 8-byte long aligned to 8 sits at an address such as 0x1008, not 0x1003.

definition: A restricted processor privilege level for ordinary applications. Page permissions and privileged-instruction rules isolate protected resources; an OS may explicitly allow device access or shared mappings rather than prohibiting every direct hardware access.
The privileged CPU mode the operating system kernel runs in, where it can manage memory, devices and interrupts.
Application binary interface: the platform rules compiled code must follow to work together, including calling conventions, type sizes, struct layout and how system calls are made.
example: The System V AMD64 ABI says the first integer argument arrives in rdi.

definition: Overlapping the steps of several instructions, like an assembly line, so a new instruction can start before the previous one finishes.
A processor design that can issue and complete more than one instruction per clock cycle.

Executing ready instructions ahead of older blocked instructions while preserving the ISA’s required observable behaviour, including exceptions and its memory-ordering rules. This does not imply sequential consistency across threads.
A memory-ordering guarantee that all threads see memory operations in one single interleaved order consistent with each thread’s program order. Most real CPUs promise something weaker.

Rules specifying which memory-access behaviours and orderings are allowed. An ISA memory model constrains hardware observations; C and C++ also impose language-level rules, including data-race restrictions, so valid concurrent source code must satisfy both layers.
The performance limit caused by instructions and data sharing one path to memory, named by John Backus in 1977. Caches and prefetching reduce it.
A design with separate memories and buses for instructions and data, so both can be accessed at once. Common in microcontrollers and DSPs.
example: An AVR microcontroller keeps its program in flash memory and its data in SRAM.

definition: A design that combines separate instruction and data paths or caches with some shared storage or address space. Split L1 instruction/data caches and unified lower memory are a common general-purpose example; the exact hierarchy is implementation-specific.
A small computer on one chip, with CPU, memory and input/output, used to control devices.
Digital signal processor: a processor specialised for fast arithmetic on streams of samples such as audio or radio signals.
A family of 8-bit microcontrollers (originally Atmel, now Microchip) with a Harvard architecture, used in classic Arduino boards.
example: The classic Arduino Uno Rev3 uses an ATmega328P AVR chip.

definition: An open-source family of microcontroller boards and software; the classic boards use AVR chips.
Non-volatile memory that keeps its contents without power; microcontrollers often store their program in it.
Static RAM: fast memory that holds each bit in a small circuit of transistors as long as power is on. Used for caches and microcontroller data memory.
Dynamic random-access memory: memory that stores bits as charge and needs refresh. It is widely used for main memory; access latency and bandwidth depend on the device, controller and access pattern.
The smallest, fastest cache, closest to each core. Most general-purpose cores split it into an instruction cache (L1i) and a data cache (L1d).
A cache that holds recently fetched instructions. After writing new code, a program may need cache maintenance so the instruction cache does not keep running the old bytes.
A cache that holds recently used data (as opposed to instructions).
Larger, slower caches between the L1 caches and main memory, usually holding both instructions and data. L3 is often shared by several cores.

Explicit operations that make caches agree with memory, for example cleaning data caches and invalidating instruction caches after writing code, plus a synchronisation step so the core fetches the new instructions.
Fetching data or instructions into cache before they are requested, based on predicted access patterns, to hide memory latency.
A compiler that turns code into machine instructions while the program runs, writes them into memory and then jumps to them.
example: V8 compiles hot JavaScript functions to native code at run time.

definition: Google’s open-source JavaScript engine, used in Chrome and Node.js, which compiles JavaScript to machine code at run time.
The main Java virtual machine implementation, which interprets bytecode and JIT-compiles frequently run methods to machine code.
Java virtual machine: the runtime that executes Java bytecode, by interpreting it or compiling it to native code.

Write xor execute: a policy forbidding a memory mapping from being writable and executable simultaneously. Separate writable and executable aliases can satisfy that mapping-level rule while still exposing executable backing memory to writes; stronger policies may forbid those aliases.
example: A JIT writes code into a read-write page, then switches it to read-execute before jumping in.

definition: A flag on Apple platforms for mmap that creates memory a JIT may switch between writable and executable, under Apple’s per-thread write-protection rules.
On Apple platforms, a signed permission in an app’s code signature that unlocks a restricted capability, such as JIT memory.
An open-source machine emulator and virtualiser that can run programs built for one ISA on another.
QEMU’s Tiny Code Generator: it translates blocks of guest instructions into host machine code and caches them, instead of interpreting each guest instruction.
Software that imitates another machine, so programs written for that machine can run on different hardware.
The wires (or links) that carry addresses and data between the CPU and memory.
Read, write and execute rights the operating system sets for each page of memory through the page tables. The CPU checks them on every access and faults on a violation.
Intel’s instruction set family, dating back to the 8086 of 1978, with variable-length instructions; its 64-bit extension is x86-64.
The 64-bit extension of x86, designed by AMD and implemented by AMD and Intel. Baseline x86-64 has 16 general-purpose 64-bit registers and instructions 1 to 15 bytes long.
The 64-bit execution state of the Arm architecture, whose instruction set is A64. Used in phones, Apple M-series Macs and many servers.
The instruction set used in ARM64 (AArch64) state: every instruction is exactly 32 bits long.
example: `add x0, x0, x1` assembles to the single 32-bit word 0x8b010000.

definition: The 32-bit execution state of the Arm architecture, with the A32 (ARM) and T32 (Thumb) instruction sets.
Intel Advanced Performance Extensions: an x86-64 extension that doubles the general-purpose registers from 16 to 32 and adds three-operand forms, using the new REX2 and extended EVEX prefixes.
On ARM64, register number 31 in many instructions: it always reads as 0 and discards anything written to it.
example: `mov x8, xzr` sets x8 to zero.

definition: The register holding the address of the top of the call stack: rsp on x86-64, sp on ARM64. Pushing moves it to lower addresses; popping moves it back.
example: `push rbx` subtracts 8 from rsp and stores rbx there.

definition: AMD’s family of x86-64 microarchitectures used in Ryzen, Threadripper and EPYC processors.
Intel’s line of x86-64 processors and their microarchitectures.
Apple’s ARM64 system-on-chip processors for Macs and iPads, starting with the M1 in 2020.
Amazon Web Services’ own ARM64 server processors.
One tick of the processor clock, the basic time step of a CPU. At 3 GHz one cycle lasts about 0.33 nanoseconds.
The length of one clock cycle, in seconds: 1 divided by the clock rate. A 1 GHz clock has a 1 ns period.
A frequency of 10^9 cycles per second. A 3 GHz CPU clock ticks three billion times a second.
One billionth of a second. Processor clock periods and memory latencies are often expressed in nanoseconds; a particular memory access latency requires a specified system.
A data rate of 10^9 bytes per second, used for memory bandwidth.
example: A DDR4-3200 channel carrying 64 data bits per transfer has a theoretical peak of 25.6 GB/s.

definition: The fourth generation of double-data-rate DRAM. DDR4-3200 makes 3.2 billion transfers per second; over a 64-bit (8-byte) channel that is a theoretical 25.6 GB/s.

An independent data path between a memory controller and memory devices. More channels can increase aggregate peak bandwidth when populated and used appropriately; realised speed depends on the workload and controller.
A group of 8 bits, the unit in which memory is addressed on x86-64 and ARM64. It can hold 256 different values.
Base-16 notation using digits 0–9 and a–f, usually written with a 0x prefix. One hex digit is exactly 4 bits, so it is a compact way to write addresses and bit patterns.
The usual way to store signed integers in binary: a negative value v in k bits is stored as the unsigned pattern v + 2^k. It makes addition the same circuit for signed and unsigned numbers.
example: −1 in 32 bits is 0xffffffff.

definition: A binary memory-size unit equal to 1024 bytes. Four kibibytes is 4096 bytes, one supported page size on many systems; page size is not universally four kibibytes.
The most significant bit of a two’s-complement number: 1 for negative values, 0 otherwise.
Complex instruction set computer: an ISA style where single instructions can do a lot (for example load, add and store in one) and instructions have many lengths. x86 is the main example.

Reduced instruction set computer: a design tradition favouring regular encodings, registers and separate ordinary memory transfers. Compressed encodings, atomics and specialised instructions mean these are tendencies rather than universal restrictions.
Digital Equipment Corporation’s 32-bit minicomputer ISA from the late 1970s, a classic heavily CISC design.
A CISC processor family from 1979, used in early Macs, the Amiga and the Atari ST.
An experimental IBM processor from the late 1970s, led by John Cocke, that pioneered RISC ideas.
A RISC research project at UC Berkeley in the early 1980s that led to the SPARC architecture.
A RISC ISA from Sun Microsystems, derived from Berkeley RISC.
A RISC ISA that grew out of John Hennessy’s research at Stanford; widely used in embedded devices and taught in textbooks.
An open, royalty-free RISC ISA started at UC Berkeley in 2010, with a small base and optional extensions such as C (compressed instructions).
IBM’s RISC ISA family, used in IBM servers and, as PowerPC, in older Macs and game consoles.

An ISA design in which ordinary arithmetic operates on registers or immediate constants, and separate instructions transfer data to and from memory. Specialised atomic read-modify-write instructions can be exceptions.
example: ARM64 needs `ldr`, `add`, `str` to increment a value in memory.

definition: An instruction that copies a value from memory into a register, such as ARM64 `ldr` or x86 `mov rax, [rdi]`.
An instruction that copies a register value into memory, such as ARM64 `str` or x86 `mov [rdi], rax`.
An encoding in which every instruction has the same size. From a known aligned instruction boundary, the following boundaries are found at that fixed spacing; A64 instructions are all 32 bits.
An instruction encoding in which instructions have different sizes, saving space for common instructions but making it harder to find where each one starts. x86 instructions are 1 to 15 bytes.

Saving a register-held value into memory, often a stack slot, when the compiler needs that register for another purpose. The value may be reloaded later; register pressure and allocation decisions determine whether spills occur.

A memory operation that reads a value and writes an updated value. An atomic read-modify-write makes that update indivisible with respect to relevant competing accesses; an ordinary read-modify-write sequence need not be atomic.
A simple internal operation that a CPU breaks an instruction into. Many x86 cores turn one complex instruction into several micro-ops before executing them.
A constant written directly inside an instruction’s encoding, rather than read from a register or memory. Its size is limited by the bits the encoding sets aside.
example: In `add x0, x0, #5` the 5 is an immediate.

definition: A block of constants placed near the code, which instructions load with a PC-relative load when a value is too big to fit in an immediate field.

Forming an address relative to an architecture-defined program-counter reference point. AArch64 ADR uses the current instruction; x86-64 RIP-relative memory operands use the next instruction. Fixed offsets within a relocated module support position independence.

AArch64 move-wide instructions: MOVZ inserts a sixteen-bit immediate and clears other bits; MOVK replaces one sixteen-bit chunk and preserves the rest. The available shift positions depend on whether the destination is 32 or 64 bits; up to four instructions build any 64-bit value.
ARM64’s compact immediate format for logical instructions: a repeating, rotated run of ones within an element of 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 or 64 bits. It can encode many masks, but not all-zeros or all-ones.
example: 0xff00ff00ff00ff00 repeats every 16 bits, so it is encodable.

definition: Logical shift left: move bits left and fill vacated positions with zeros. For a fixed-width unsigned value this multiplies by a power of two modulo that width’s range; high bits can be lost. AArch64 can shift an operand within many instructions.
example: `x1, lsl #2` means x1 × 4.

definition: A shift that fills vacated positions with zeros. Unsigned right shift divides by the corresponding power of two and rounds down; fixed-width left shift can discard high bits, so multiplication may wrap.
A right shift that copies the sign bit into the vacated bits, so negative numbers stay negative. It divides by 2^n but rounds towards minus infinity.
example: Arithmetic-shifting −7 right by 1 gives −4.

definition: A one-byte x86-64 prefix in the range 0x40–0x4F. Its W bit requests 64-bit operand size where that encoding uses it, and its R/X/B bits extend applicable register fields; instruction-specific rules still apply.
example: The 48 in `48 01 f8` is a REX prefix with W = 1.

definition: A two-byte x86 prefix introduced with Intel APX that lets instructions name the extra registers r16–r31.
An x86 prefix family introduced with AVX that encodes three-operand vector instructions compactly.
A four-byte x86 prefix introduced with AVX-512 that encodes 512-bit vector instructions, mask registers and (with APX) extended general-purpose registers.
Bytes placed before an x86 opcode that modify it, for example the lock and rep prefixes, operand-size overrides, REX or VEX.

An x86 encoding byte with mod, reg and r/m fields. Together with the opcode and prefixes it selects register or memory addressing; reg can name a register or extend the opcode, and r/m can require a SIB byte or a special addressing form.
example: ModRM f8 = 11 111 000: register form, reg = rdi, rm = rax.

definition: Scale-index-base: an optional x86 byte that describes a memory operand of the form base + index × scale, with scale 1, 2, 4 or 8.
A constant byte offset written into an instruction and added to a base address, for example the 8 in `[rdi + 8]`.

The encoding bytes that identify an x86 operation together with applicable prefixes and opcode-extension fields. A familiar legacy form uses one to three opcode bytes, but this is not the complete modern encoding grammar.
example: 01 is the opcode for ADD r/m64, r64.

definition: An instruction form where one operand is both a source and the destination, so the old value is overwritten. Most legacy x86 arithmetic works this way.
example: `add rax, rdi` computes rax + rdi into rax.

definition: An instruction form with a separately encoded destination and two source operands. Distinct source registers remain unchanged, but choosing the same register for a source and destination still overwrites that register.
example: `add x0, x1, x2` leaves x1 and x2 unchanged.

definition: How many bytes a program’s instructions take. Denser code fits more in the instruction cache.
The CPU step that works out what an instruction’s bits mean: operation, registers, constants and length.
A compressed instruction set for 32-bit ARM that mixes 16-bit and 32-bit instructions to improve code density.
Short (usually 16-bit) encodings of common instructions added to a fixed-length RISC ISA to improve code density, such as RISC-V’s C extension.
A rule for where an instruction’s operand comes from: a constant, a register, or a memory address computed from registers and offsets.
The memory address an addressing mode actually computes, for example base + index × scale + displacement.
example: `[rdi + rsi*4 + 8]` with rdi = 0x1000 and rsi = 3 gives 0x1014.

definition: Using the value in a register as the memory address, as in `[rdi]` or `[x0]`.
An address formed by adding a constant offset to a base register: used for struct fields and stack slots.
example: `[rsp + 24]` reads a stack slot 24 bytes above rsp.

definition: An address formed as base + index × scale, so an array element can be reached by its index directly. x86 scales are 1, 2, 4 or 8.
ARM64 addressing forms that also update the base register: pre-index adds the offset before the access (`[x0, #8]!`), post-index after it (`[x0], #8`).
example: `ldr w9, [x0], #4` loads from x0, then adds 4 to x0.

definition: x86’s load effective address instruction: it computes an address expression and puts the number in a register without accessing memory or changing flags. Compilers use it for cheap arithmetic.
example: `lea rax, [rdi + rdi*4 + 7]` computes 5 × rdi + 7.

definition: Run time = instructions executed × average cycles per instruction × clock period. It shows why fewer instructions do not automatically mean faster code.
Cycles per instruction: the average number of clock cycles each instruction takes in a given program.

Machine code designed to work at permitted load addresses without rewriting its instruction bytes. It commonly uses PC-relative references and runtime-resolved pointer tables; encoding reach and platform relocation rules still impose limits.

Advanced Vector Extensions: x86 instruction extensions using VEX encodings, including operations on 128- and 256-bit vectors. AVX-512 adds EVEX-encoded forms, mask registers and operations on up to 512-bit vectors; supported widths and instructions depend on extensions.
ARM64 instructions that load or store two registers at once, commonly used to save and restore register pairs in function prologues and epilogues.
example: `stp x29, x30, [sp, #-16]!` pushes the frame pointer and link register.

definition: Instructions that speed up common cryptographic algorithms such as AES and SHA.

A textual notation for machine instructions, normally using operation and register names, together with labels and assembler directives. Pseudoinstructions and aliases mean one source line need not correspond to exactly one encoded instruction.
example: `add rax, rdi` is the assembly for the bytes 48 01 f8.

definition: The Linux performance-analysis tool. `perf record` samples where a program spends time and `perf annotate` shows the hot instructions.
Extra data in a binary that maps machine code back to source files, lines, functions and variables, used by debuggers and profilers.
A website (godbolt.org) that shows the assembly produced by many compilers for code you type, with matching lines coloured.
Turning a loop over single values into SIMD instructions that process several elements at once.
Working out how a program works from its compiled binary, usually by reading its disassembly.
A tool that turns machine-code bytes back into assembly text, such as objdump or a debugger’s disassemble command.
The x86-64 accumulator register. It holds integer return values in the System V and Windows conventions; eax, ax and al are its low 32, 16 and 8 bits.
An x86-64 general-purpose register that is callee-saved in the System V ABI, so it survives function calls. ebx is its low 32 bits.
An x86-64 general-purpose register: the fourth integer argument in System V, the first on Windows x64. ecx is its low 32 bits.

An x86-64 general-purpose register: the third ordinary integer argument in System V AMD64 and the high half of a returned 128-bit integer. Other 128-bit result types have different ABI rules; edx and dl name its low 32 and 8 bits.
An x86-64 general-purpose register: the second integer argument in System V. esi is its low 32 bits.
An x86-64 general-purpose register: the first integer argument in System V. edi and dil are its low 32 and 8 bits.
The eight extra general-purpose registers x86-64 added. In System V, r8 and r9 carry the 5th and 6th integer arguments, r10 and r11 are scratch, and r12–r15 are callee-saved.

The first ARM64 general-purpose register: it carries the first integer argument and the integer return value under AAPCS64; w0 names its low 32 bits. (On RISC-V, x0 is instead a register that always reads as zero.)

ARM64’s general-purpose registers: x0–x30 are 64 bits wide, and w0–w30 name their low 32 bits. Writing a w register zeroes the upper 32 bits. RISC-V also names its 32 integer registers x0–x31, with different conventions.
The x86-64 128-bit SSE registers, used for floating-point and vector values. System V passes floating-point arguments in xmm0–xmm7 and returns them in xmm0.

AArch64’s 32 SIMD and floating-point registers V0–V31, each 128 bits. D0 is the low 64-bit view of V0, often used for a double-precision value; base AAPCS64 uses V0–V7 for applicable floating-point arguments.
An x86 assembly notation written destination first, with plain register names and memory as [base + index*scale + disp]. Used by Intel and Microsoft documentation and by `objdump -M intel`.
example: `sub rax, rdi` means rax = rax − rdi.

definition: An x86 assembly notation used by default in GNU tools: source first and destination last, % before registers, $ before constants, and memory as disp(base,index,scale).
example: `subq %rdi, %rax` means rax = rax − rdi.

definition: The GNU debugger: it runs programs under control, sets breakpoints and shows registers, memory and disassembly.
A GNU binutils tool that displays information from object files and executables, including disassembly (`objdump -d`) and relocations (`-r`).
A GNU binutils tool that prints the structure of ELF files: headers, sections, segments, symbols and dynamic entries.
The assembler from GNU binutils, used by GCC to turn .s files into object files.
Intel-syntax words that say how many bytes a memory operand covers: byte = 1, word = 2, dword (double word) = 4, qword (quad word) = 8.
example: `dword ptr [rdi]` reads 4 bytes.

definition: Single-bit status results such as zero, sign, carry and overflow that applicable arithmetic and compare instructions record for later conditions. x86 stores these among the other status/control bits of RFLAGS; AArch64 has the NZCV flags.
AArch64’s Negative, Zero, Carry and oVerflow condition flags. Instructions such as CMP, SUBS and ADDS update them; architectural status-register writes can change them too.
The flag set when an instruction’s result is zero. Equal-comparisons test it: `je`/`jz` jump when it is 1.
The flag set when an unsigned addition carries out of the top bit or (on x86) a subtraction needs a borrow. Unsigned comparisons such as `ja` and `jb` read it.
The x86 flag that copies the top (sign) bit of a result, so it is 1 for negative signed results.
The flag set when a result is too big or too small for a signed number of that width. Signed comparisons such as `jg` combine it with the sign flag.
Compare: subtracts the second operand from the first, sets the condition flags and throws the result away.
example: `cmp rcx, rsi` then `jne` loops while rcx ≠ rsi.

definition: x86 test (ARM64 tst): bitwise-ANDs two operands, sets the flags and discards the result. `test rax, rax` checks for zero or negative.
An instruction that may change the program counter. A conditional branch jumps only if a condition (usually on the flags) holds; otherwise execution falls through to the next instruction.
A branch to a lower address, earlier in the code. It is the usual sign of a loop.
A jump or call whose target address comes from a register or memory rather than being written in the instruction. They are harder to predict and a target for attacks.
example: `jmp rax` jumps to whatever address rax holds.

definition: The family of x86 conditional jumps (je, jne, jg, ja and so on), and ARM64’s b.cond equivalents. The suffix (condition code) says which flag combination to test.
x86 instructions that write 1 or 0 to a byte register depending on a condition code, turning a comparison into a number without branching.
example: `setg dl` sets dl to 1 if the last comparison was “greater”.

definition: x86 conditional move: copies a value only if a condition holds, letting compilers avoid a branch.
ARM64 conditional select family: csel picks one of two registers, cset writes 1 or 0, cinc conditionally adds 1 and cneg conditionally negates, all based on the flags.
example: `csel w0, w0, w1, gt` returns the larger of w0 and w1 after a compare.

definition: Whether bits are read as a signed (two’s complement) or unsigned number. The same register bits can mean −1 or 4,294,967,295; signed and unsigned comparisons use different condition codes.
Widening a value by filling the new upper bits with zeros, the correct way to widen an unsigned number.
example: `mov eax, edi` zero-extends edi into all 64 bits of rax.

definition: Widening a signed value by copying its sign bit into the new upper bits, so the number keeps its value.
example: −1 in 32 bits (0xffffffff) sign-extends to 0xffffffffffffffff.

definition: Hardware that guesses the outcome and target of a branch before it is known, so the pipeline can keep fetching. Wrong guesses cost work.

A wrong prediction of a branch’s outcome or target. The core redirects execution and discards incorrect speculative work; cost depends on the microarchitecture and workload rather than a universal cycle count.
A variable that changes by a fixed amount each loop iteration, such as the index i in a for loop.
Setting a register to zero with `xor eax, eax`: a 2-byte encoding that many cores recognise as independent of the old value.

No-operation instruction: it advances execution without changing ordinary program results. It still occupies instruction bytes and can consume frontend or execution resources; multi-byte x86 NOP forms do not access their apparent memory operand.
An x86 instruction that marks a valid target for indirect jumps and calls under Intel CET indirect-branch tracking; on older CPUs it behaves as a NOP.
The 1999 revision of the C standard. It fixed integer division to truncate towards zero.
The 2018 revision of the C standard (ISO/IEC 9899:2018), mainly corrections to C11.
Behaviour the C standard leaves to each compiler, which must document its choice, such as right-shifting a negative signed integer.
Program behaviour the C or C++ standard places no requirements on, such as signed integer overflow or out-of-bounds access. Compilers may assume it never happens.

A compiler setting selecting groups of optimisation passes. GCC -O0 disables most optimisation for a useful debugging experience; -O2 and -O3 enable additional transformations. Exact passes and output depend on compiler version, target and other flags.

A compiler transformation that replaces integer division by a known constant with a suitable multiply, shift and adjustment sequence. The correct sequence depends on width, signedness and rounding; target costs determine whether it is useful.
The most negative value of C’s int type, −2,147,483,648 for 32-bit int. It has no positive counterpart, so negating it overflows.
The number of 1 bits in a value. x86 has a popcnt instruction; Kernighan’s method clears the lowest set bit with x & (x − 1) once per 1 bit.
example: 44 = 0b101100 has a population count of 3.

definition: Multiply instructions: x86 imul (signed multiply) and mul on ARM64 and RISC-V.
The part of an ABI that says how functions call each other: where arguments and return values go, which registers a call may destroy, and how the stack is laid out.
The C, C++ and Objective-C compiler front end of the LLVM project.
The GNU Compiler Collection, including the gcc C compiler driver, which runs the preprocessor, compiler, assembler and linker for you.
Go’s mechanism for calling C code, which must translate between Go’s and the platform’s calling conventions.
The error (signal SIGSEGV on Unix) a program gets when it accesses memory it is not allowed to, for example an unmapped address or a stack overflow into a guard page.
The address of the instruction after a call, where execution should continue when the called function returns. x86-64 pushes it on the stack; ARM64 puts it in the link register.

A register used for a return address; AArch64 BL writes X30, and RET uses X30 by default. A function making a nested call must preserve its original return address if it will later return to its caller normally.
The ARM64 call instruction: it stores the address of the next instruction in x30 (the link register) and jumps to the target.
example: `bl printf` sets x30, then jumps to printf.

definition: The ordinary near x86-64 CALL saves the next instruction’s address on the stack and transfers control to its target. A 64-bit near call subtracts eight from RSP to store that return address; other control-transfer forms have their own rules.
example: `call f` subtracts 8 from rsp, stores the next instruction’s address there, then jumps to f.

definition: A return instruction. An ordinary near x86-64 RET pops a return address into RIP; AArch64 RET branches through X30 by default, or another explicitly named register. Protection features can add checks.
x86 stack instructions that store or retrieve a stack operand and adjust the stack pointer. A normal 64-bit PUSH or POP changes RSP by eight bytes; operand-size variants have different widths.

A function that makes no further function calls. A non-leaf function does make calls; on AArch64 a leaf often needs no stack save of its incoming link register, but its own other requirements can still need a frame.
The calling convention and ABI used for x86-64 on Linux, macOS and the BSDs: integer arguments in rdi, rsi, rdx, rcx, r8, r9; results in rax; 16-byte stack alignment at calls; a 128-byte red zone.

aliases: Procedure Call Standard for the Arm 64-bit Architecture
definition: Arm’s procedure call standard for ARM64: integer arguments in x0–x7, results in x0, callee-saved x19–x28, and x8 for an indirect result pointer. Platforms such as Apple’s add their own variations.
Apple’s variant of AAPCS64. Among other differences, anonymous variadic arguments always go on the stack and x18 is reserved.
A function that takes a variable number of arguments, such as C’s printf.
A C type that groups several named fields into one block of memory, each field at a fixed offset.
A type built from several values, such as a struct or array. ABIs have special rules for passing and returning them.

Homogeneous floating-point aggregate: an AAPCS64 aggregate whose one to four fundamental members have the same floating-point base type. Qualifying results use floating-point/vector registers; argument allocation also depends on the remaining register slots and ABI rules.
example: struct { double x, y, z; } is an HFA returned in d0–d2.

definition: A way of returning a large value: the caller provides memory and passes its address as a hidden argument (rdi in System V, x8 in AAPCS64); the callee writes the result there.
A register a called function may overwrite freely. If the caller needs the value afterwards, the caller must save it.
example: In System V, rax, rcx, rdx, rsi, rdi and r8–r11 are caller-saved.

definition: A register a called function must give back unchanged; if it wants to use one, it saves the old value in its prologue and restores it in its epilogue.
example: In System V, rbx, rbp and r12–r15 are callee-saved.

definition: The instructions at the start of a function that set up its stack frame: saving callee-saved registers, setting the frame pointer and reserving space.

The instructions at the end of a function that undo its prologue (restore registers, free the frame) before returning. By analogy, the clean-up code after an unrolled or vectorised loop is sometimes called a loop epilogue.
ARM64 register x18, which AAPCS64 lets a platform reserve; Apple platforms and Windows do, so portable code should not use it.
ARM64 registers x16 and x17, scratch registers that linker-generated stubs (veneers and PLT code) may overwrite between a call and its target.
The region of the call stack belonging to one active function call: its return address, saved registers, local variables and outgoing arguments.
The region of memory that holds one stack frame per active function call. It grows towards lower addresses on x86-64 and ARM64.

A register such as RBP on x86-64 or X29 on AArch64 used as a stable reference into a function’s stack frame. When compatible frame records are maintained, saved frame pointers form a chain that debuggers can walk; optimised code may omit this chain.
On ARM64, the pair of saved x29 and x30 values a function stores in its frame; x29 points at it, linking frames into a chain.

A reconstruction of the active function calls at a point in a program, often using frame pointers or unwind metadata. Optimisation and available debug information affect which physical or logical calls can be displayed.
Recovering the caller frames from the current stack, using frame pointers or separate metadata that describes each function’s frame layout.

Under the System V AMD64 ABI, the 128 bytes below the current stack pointer that signal or interrupt handlers must not disturb in conforming user-space execution. Functions can use it for temporary values not needed across calls; it is not a Linux kernel-stack guarantee.
Streaming SIMD Extensions: x86 instructions on the 128-bit xmm registers. Aligned forms such as movaps fault on addresses that are not multiples of 16.
A function the operating system runs in a process when a signal (such as SIGSEGV or SIGINT) is delivered, interrupting normal execution.
Microsoft’s x86-64 calling convention: integer arguments in rcx, rdx, r8, r9; 32 bytes of shadow space; rsi, rdi and xmm6–xmm15 callee-saved; no red zone.
The 32 bytes a Windows x64 caller must reserve on the stack above the return address, one 8-byte slot for each of the four register arguments.
A compatibility layer that runs Windows programs on Linux and macOS, translating between Windows and Unix conventions.
A call that is a function’s last action. The compiler can tear down the current frame and jump to the target, which then returns straight to the original caller.
n! = n × (n − 1) × … × 1, with 0! = 1. It grows very fast: 20! is about 2.4 × 10^18.

A signed arithmetic result outside its type’s representable range. Ordinary C signed arithmetic overflow has undefined behaviour; unsigned integer arithmetic instead reduces modulo its width’s range. Instruction-level wrapping does not define overflowing C code.
example: For a 32-bit signed int, adding one to 2,147,483,647 overflows; a 32-bit unsigned addition wraps modulo 4,294,967,296.

definition: A C declaration giving a function’s return type and parameter types, allowing calls to be checked and argument passing to follow the ABI. In C versions before C23 an empty parameter list is not a prototype for a no-argument function.

A group of registers used for one kind of value, such as integer registers versus floating-point/vector registers. System V AMD64 and base AAPCS64 allocate ordinary scalar arguments separately by class; Windows x64 instead shares the first four argument positions across classes.
An inaccessible page placed next to a stack so that running off its end causes a fault instead of silently overwriting other memory.
A type whose required alignment is stricter than the platform’s normal maximum, for example a 32-byte-aligned vector.
A compiler step that translates a higher-level construct (a loop, a switch, a struct access) into simpler operations such as compares, branches, loads and stores.
The data model used by 64-bit Unix systems: int is 32 bits, while long and pointers are 64 bits. ILP32, by contrast, makes int, long and pointers all 32 bits.

Rewriting loop control so that an entry test can guard a bottom-tested body. This can reduce branches on the common iteration path while preserving the original zero-iteration case; exact generated code is target-dependent.
A loop whose body runs first and whose condition is tested at the end, so it always runs at least once unless guarded.
A compiler optimisation that replaces an expensive operation with a cheaper one, such as turning a multiply by the loop index into adding a constant each iteration.
Repeating a loop body several times per iteration to reduce loop overhead, with extra code for leftover iterations.

Moving or reusing a computation outside a loop when its result is invariant and doing so preserves the language’s observable behaviour. Possible memory effects, exceptions and profitability can prevent the transformation.

Two ways of laying out multidimensional arrays: row-major stores each complete row consecutively, while column-major stores each complete column consecutively. C uses row-major order; Fortran uses column-major order.
example: In int a[8][10], a[2][3] is element number 2 × 10 + 3 = 23.

definition: Bytes inserted between structure members or after the last member to meet layout/alignment rules. For ordinary System V LP64 scalar structs, tail padding aligns successive array elements; padding contents are not a portable serialisation format.
example: Under ordinary System V LP64 layout, struct { char c; int x; } is eight bytes: one field byte, three padding bytes and four int bytes.

definition: The C operator giving a type’s or object’s size in bytes, including any padding.
A C macro giving the byte offset of a field from the start of its struct.
A check evaluated at compile time; the build fails if it is false. Useful to pin down struct sizes and offsets.
The constant distance in bytes from the start of a struct to one of its fields, known at compile time and used as a displacement.
example: `p->v` at offset 8 becomes `[rdi + 8]`.

definition: The distance in bytes from one array element to the next, equal to the element size (including padding).
A table of code addresses or offsets indexed by a value, used with one indirect jump to dispatch a dense switch statement.
Switch cases are dense when their values fill a small range with few gaps (suiting a jump table), and sparse when they are widely spread (suiting compares).

A table that maps each input (an index or key) directly to a stored result, so the answer is looked up instead of computed or chosen by branches. In machine code it is usually an array indexed by the input value, read with one load.
A family of attacks, disclosed in 2018, that trick a CPU into speculatively executing code that leaks secrets through cache timing; indirect branches are one avenue.

A return-trampoline technique used on specified processors to mitigate speculative indirect-branch target injection. Its suitability depends on the processor and other mitigations; it is not a universal guarantee against branch-predictor or speculative-execution attacks.
When two pointers or references may refer to overlapping memory. A compiler must assume a store through one may change what the other reads, which blocks some optimisations.

A C pointer qualifier that creates an access-based promise within an execution of its associated block. For an object modified through a restrict-based pointer, relevant accesses must obey the standard’s based-on rules; it does not simply say all pointer addresses differ.
A graph of a function’s basic blocks (straight-line runs of instructions) and the jumps between them. A loop shows up as a cycle.
A test that an index or value lies within an allowed range before it is used, for example before indexing an array or a switch statement's jump table.
An array indexed by two or more numbers, such as a[row][column]; C stores it as one flat block in row-major order.
Position-independent executable: a program built as position-independent code so the loader can place it at a random address under ASLR.
A GCC and Clang option that stops switch statements being compiled into jump tables, used by some kernels to avoid indirect branches.
The first compilation stage for C: it expands #include and #define directives, producing plain C source.
The program that turns assembly text into machine code in an object file, recording relocations for addresses it does not yet know.
The program that combines object files and libraries into an executable or shared library: it resolves symbols, lays out sections and patches relocations.
One C source file after preprocessing: the unit a compiler processes at a time in separate compilation.
Optimising across source files at link time, by keeping compiler intermediate code in object files instead of only machine code.

Platform C-runtime startup object files, such as crt1.o and crti.o, normally selected by a compiler driver for an ordinary hosted executable. They supply entry or initialisation machinery; options such as -nostartfiles and other runtime models can omit or replace them.

A relocatable object contains code/data sections, symbol information and relocation records for later linking. Conventional ELF ET_REL files are linker inputs rather than directly executable images; specialised loaders can also consume relocatable objects.

Executable and Linkable Format: a file format used by Linux and several other operating systems for relocatable objects, executables, shared objects and core files. It is not the executable format of every Unix-family system.
A named region of an ELF file used by linkers and tools: .text holds code, .rodata constants, .data initialised globals and .bss zero-initialised globals.
The list in an object file of names it defines (such as main) and names it uses but does not define (such as puts, marked undefined).
A record that tells the linker or loader to patch a particular location with an address once the address is known, for example a call displacement to puts.
example: R_X86_64_PLT32 puts-0x4 asks for a PC-relative distance to puts with addend −4.

definition: An x86-64 relocation type for calls: the linker writes the PC-relative distance to the function's PLT stub (or the function itself, when it can call it directly), computed as target + addend − field address.
A constant stored in a relocation that is added when computing the value to patch in, such as the −4 that turns a field-relative distance into an instruction-end-relative one.

A library that a runtime loader maps into processes using it. Unchanged file-backed code pages can be shared; replacing a compatible library normally benefits newly started processes while existing mappings may retain the old version.
example: libc.so.6 is the C library most Linux programs share.

definition: A file recording a process’s memory and registers when it crashed, for later debugging.

A collection of object files such as libfoo.a. Traditional GNU ld extracts members needed for unresolved references when it searches that archive; order, archive groups, whole-archive options and linker choice change extraction behaviour.

A symbol with weak binding, whose definition can yield to a suitable strong definition. Under relevant ELF linking rules an unresolved weak reference can have a zero value rather than causing the usual undefined-reference error; it is distinct from a strong definition.

Matching symbol references with definitions under the linker or dynamic loader’s binding, visibility, interposition and input-order rules. Required unresolved references or conflicting strong definitions can cause errors; weak references and dynamic imports have exceptions.
The traditional linker from GNU binutils.
An ELF linker developed within GNU Binutils. It is a distinct implementation from GNU ld; availability and maintenance status depend on the selected Binutils release and build.

The LLVM project’s linker family, supporting formats including ELF, PE/COFF and Mach-O. Its ELF linker aims for GNU-linker compatibility, but input-order behaviour and supported options can differ; performance depends on the workload.
A modern, highly parallel linker for ELF files on Linux and other Unix-like systems.
A collection of compiler and toolchain components, including the Clang compiler and the LLD linker.

Including linked library code in the executable instead of depending on those shared-library files for that code. A fully static executable can still need runtime files, devices or configuration, and incorporated library fixes require a rebuilt or relinked executable.

An ELF program header describes a runtime segment or other loader metadata. PT_LOAD entries specify memory mappings and permissions; entries such as PT_INTERP and GNU_RELRO describe different roles and do not each create an independent mapping.
An ELF program header that names the dynamic loader the kernel must map to run the program, such as /lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2.
An ELF program header whose flags tell Linux whether the program needs an executable stack; RW without E requests a non-executable stack.
An ELF program header marking a range the dynamic loader makes read-only after relocation, such as the GOT under full RELRO.
Shorthand for memory permissions: R read, W write, X (or E) execute. RWX memory is writable and executable at once, which hardened systems avoid.
Resolving a program’s references to shared libraries when it is loaded or run, rather than copying the library code in at build time.
The program (ld.so on Linux) that maps a dynamically linked program’s shared libraries, performs relocations and then starts the program.
An entry in an ELF file’s dynamic section naming a shared library it depends on.
The C standard library. glibc is the GNU implementation used by most Linux distributions.

Global Offset Table: data slots used by position-independent code and linkage machinery for applicable symbol addresses. The loader fills or resolves slots; full RELRO can make protected slots read-only after relocation rather than leaving the whole table permanently writable.

Procedure Linkage Table: linkage stubs used in executables and shared objects to call applicable external functions. Classic x86-64 stubs jump through GOT slots and can invoke a resolver on the first lazily bound call; alternative binding and stub formats exist.

Deferring applicable dynamic function-symbol resolution until the function’s first call. This can avoid startup lookup work for unused functions, but library mapping and other relocation work can still occur at startup.

Resolving applicable required dynamic symbol relocations when an object loads rather than waiting for its first call. This permits protected GOT slots to become read-only under full RELRO, but does not pre-resolve every possible future dynamic lookup.

Relocation read-only: the linker identifies a GNU_RELRO range, and the dynamic loader protects that range after relocation. Conventional full RELRO combines this with eager binding so applicable GOT function slots can be protected too; ordinary relocated writable variables do not all become read-only.
The dynamic loader routine that, on a lazily bound call, looks a function up in the loaded libraries and writes its address into the GOT.

A Linux system call that replaces the calling process’s program image. For the ELF case it maps the executable segments and establishes startup state; executable interpreter scripts follow an interpreter path.
Key–value pairs the kernel places on a new process’s stack (page size, entry point, pointer to 16 random bytes and more) for the dynamic loader and libc.
The argument count, argument strings and environment strings a C program receives, placed on the initial stack by the kernel.

For the conventional glibc ELF C executable shown, _start is the executable’s machine entry routine and calls __libc_start_main, which eventually invokes main. A dynamic ELF interpreter can execute first; __libc_start_main is a different function, not another name for _start.
An environment variable that makes the glibc dynamic loader print what it is doing, such as library search (libs) or symbol binding (bindings).
A Linux tracing tool that can display selected system calls, their arguments and results, and signals. Filters, attachment timing and process-following options determine which events appear.
The system call that maps files or anonymous memory into a process’s address space with chosen permissions.
Freedom from bugs such as out-of-bounds access and use-after-free. Memory-safe languages (Rust’s safe subset, Java, Python) rule them out by design.

An out-of-bounds write beyond a buffer’s storage. Out-of-bounds reads are a related memory-safety error but do not write or overwrite adjacent data; a write can corrupt control data depending on layout.

An execute-disable permission in architectural page translation. With x86 support and EFER.NXE enabled, bit 63 of applicable paging entries can prohibit instruction fetches; Arm execute-never controls use different formats and names.
Data Execution Prevention: Windows’ policy of marking data pages non-executable using the NX bit.
Arm page-table bits that forbid execution at unprivileged (user) level and privileged (kernel) level respectively.

The execute-disable-enable control bit in the x86 EFER model-specific register. When supported and set, it enables execute-disable permission checking in applicable paging entries; EFER itself also contains unrelated control bits.

An entry in a virtual-memory translation structure. A leaf entry can map a page or larger block and carry permissions; a non-leaf entry can point to a lower-level table, with architecture-specific permission effects.

An attack that chains existing executable instruction fragments, commonly ending in returns, instead of injecting new instruction bytes. It is one kind of code-reuse attack; not every code-reuse technique uses returns.
An attack that places the attacker’s own instructions in memory and makes the program run them.

Address space layout randomisation varies eligible process memory locations, such as stack, heap, shared libraries and PIE executable mappings, under OS and deployment policy. It makes locations harder to predict, but leaks and limited entropy can undermine that protection.
Kernel address space layout randomisation: loading the kernel at a random base address.

A measure of uncertainty. In this module’s uniform address-choice model, b bits correspond to two to the power b equally likely positions; non-uniform distributions need a more careful entropy or guessing model.
example: 8 bits of entropy means 256 possible positions.

definition: The Linux setting /proc/sys/kernel/randomize_va_space that turns ASLR off (0), on for stack, mmap and libraries (1), or additionally for the heap (2).
A bug that reveals memory contents such as a pointer, letting an attacker defeat ASLR or read a stack canary.
Letting a definition in one loaded module (for example via LD_PRELOAD) override a symbol of the same name in another.

A GNU ELF symbol mechanism whose resolver selects a function implementation, for example one suited to CPU features. Resolution can occur during relocation or lazy binding; it is not restricted to one universal load-time moment.
A process created by fork(), starting as a copy of its parent, including its memory layout and stack canary.

A guard value stored in a protected function’s stack frame and checked before relevant exits. A mismatch can detect an overwrite crossing the guard, but an unchanged guard, a bypassing write or harm before the check can escape detection.
Memory where each thread has its own copy of a variable. On x86-64 Linux it is reached through the fs segment register; glibc keeps the stack guard there at fs:0x28.
The glibc function called when a stack canary check fails; it prints “stack smashing detected” and aborts.

Compiler options controlling stack-guard instrumentation. GCC -fstack-protector-strong covers additional functions with eligible local arrays or references to local frame addresses; -all requests every function, while -fno-stack-protector disables it. Optimised-away or register-only objects do not count.
Intel Control-flow Enforcement Technology: a hardware shadow stack for return addresses plus indirect-branch tracking with ENDBR64 landing pads.

Protected storage for return addresses, compared with the ordinary return address by supported, enabled control-transfer protection. It detects certain return-address corruption; exact checks and exceptions depend on the architecture and control-transfer form.

An Intel CET feature that, when enabled, checks applicable indirect call/jump targets for the expected ENDBR landing instruction. Architecture-defined exceptions and suppressions exist; it is not a check of every conceivable control transfer.

An Arm architectural feature that creates and checks authentication codes for pointers such as return addresses using keys and a context value. Codes can occupy pointer bits; effectiveness depends on code width, keys, context and enabled software checks.

An AArch64 feature that, when enabled for guarded executable pages, restricts applicable indirect-branch targets to compatible landing instructions. Suitable PAC instructions can also serve as landing pads in defined cases; a literal BTI mnemonic is not the only possibility.
A glibc and compiler feature that adds size checks to some library calls (such as memcpy and strcpy) when object sizes are known.

A tool that reports binary hardening indicators such as NX, PIE, RELRO, stack-protector and fortified-call evidence. Its report and command syntax depend on the version; binary metadata alone does not prove that every runtime protection is enabled.
Using several independent protections so that bypassing one does not defeat the whole system.
A range of a process’s virtual address space backed by a file or anonymous memory, with its own permissions.
The fixed-size unit (commonly 4 KiB) in which virtual memory is mapped and protected.

Establishing a virtual mapping before providing its resident backing page, then resolving a page fault when access requires it. File-backed demand paging can bring file contents into memory; anonymous memory can use zero pages or newly allocated zero-filled pages.
The C function that copies a NUL-terminated string without checking the destination’s size, a classic source of buffer overflows.
The zero byte that marks the end of a C string.

An x86-64 linear address satisfying the implemented address-width rule: upper bits normally replicate the highest address bit. Non-canonical uses can fault; enabled linear-address-masking features define exceptions for specified address uses.
The x86-64 instruction that enters the kernel for a system call; it overwrites rcx and r11.

An architectural step that makes subsequent instruction execution observe the required context and instruction stream. AArch64 ISB flushes the local pipeline as part of a correct code-update protocol; it does not by itself clean caches or synchronise all other cores.
The fixed-size block (commonly 64 bytes) in which data moves between memory and caches.

Operations connected by data dependencies: a later operation needs an earlier result. True dependent results constrain overlap, although independent work can overlap and memory prediction or speculation requires separate analysis.

AArch64 PC-relative address instructions. ADR uses a signed 21-bit byte offset from the instruction; ADRP uses a signed 21-bit offset in four-kibibyte units from the instruction’s four-kibibyte page. Their positive reaches are one encoding unit shorter than their negative reaches.
An instruction set with many general-purpose registers (ARM64 has 31), so compilers can keep more values in registers and spill less to memory.
In the System V AMD64 ABI, the classification for arguments and return values passed in memory rather than registers, such as a 24-byte struct of three longs.
Making newly written instructions the ones a core actually fetches and executes, using the platform’s cache-maintenance and instruction-synchronisation steps.

An isolated environment in which a program runs with its own view of files, processes and network, sharing the host's kernel. A container image can bundle its own copies of shared libraries, so updating the host's libraries does not update it.
example: A Docker image built on an older distribution keeps that distribution's libc.so.6 even after the host's libc is patched.

definition: Wide CPU registers used by SIMD instructions and also for floating-point values: x86 XMM has 128-bit views, AVX adds 256-bit YMM views, and AVX-512 adds 512-bit ZMM views. AArch64 V0–V31 are 128 bits; ABI rules select how these registers pass floating-point arguments.
example: System V passes a double argument in xmm0; AAPCS64 passes it in v0 (as d0).

definition: The region of a process's memory used for blocks allocated and freed at run time, for example with C's malloc and free, as opposed to the call stack.
example: Under ASLR with randomize_va_space set to 2, the start of the heap is placed at a random address.

definition: The software, centred on the kernel, that manages a computer's hardware and runs programs as processes, giving each its own memory and handling system calls. Linux, Windows and macOS are examples.
A tool that measures where a running program spends its time, often by sampling the program counter many times a second, so you can find the hot functions and instructions.
example: Linux perf is a sampling profiler.

definition: The GNU collection of tools for working with object files and executables, including the assembler (as), the linker (ld), objdump and readelf.
American computer scientist (1924–2007) who led the team that created FORTRAN. In his 1977 Turing Award lecture he named the von Neumann bottleneck.
A Linux mechanism for reading and changing kernel settings at run time, exposed as files under /proc/sys and through the sysctl command.
example: kernel.randomize_va_space is the sysctl that controls ASLR.

definition: An operating system first developed at Bell Labs around 1970, and the family of systems that follow its design and interfaces, including Linux, macOS and the BSDs.
Reading or writing outside an object’s valid storage bounds. Reads can disclose unrelated data and writes can corrupt it; neither becomes valid C merely because the machine can access the address.
An attack that redirects control through instructions already in executable memory. Return-oriented programming is one form; other forms use indirect jumps or calls instead of returns.
